newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela sees need to deal with ANC dissidents.
newsitem.headline: Mandela sees need to deal with ANC dissidents.

text.p: Half-way through its first term in office, South Africa's ruling African National Congress is struggling to maintain unity in some of its fractious regional branches.
President Nelson Mandela has intervened in some of the squabbles, but political analysts say this approach might only postpone an eventual explosion of grassroots resentment.

In Free State province Mandela removed premier Patrick Lekota to end a personality feud, and in Northern Province last week he tried -- in vain -- to ensure that premier Ngoako Ramatlhodi's position was not challenged.
In the Eastern Cape, an internal ANC document said party membership was plummeting and organisation was in tatters.
Mandela was in the Western Cape over the weekend as part of a tour of the party's provincial structures, seeking to bolster morale and nip dissent in the bud.
"The organisation is united," he told a news conference on Sunday. "Unity does not mean we don't have dissidents, the point is those dissidents are not in a position to split the organisation."
But he told ANC branch leaders "the organisational state of affairs in the ANC and its allied formations often leaves much to be desired".
"We all know that a great deal of energy has been consumed on intra-organisational leadership rivalries, personality squabbles and factionalism," he said.
Steven Friedman, director of the Centre for Policy Studies think tank, said the national leadership had to be circumspect in maintaining unity in the ANC because of the diversity of its membership.
"There's a clear pattern of saying the national level will decide what's good for the provinces," he said.

"I think that is a very severe problem for the ANC. If you accept that the ANC is an umbrella that incorporates a whole lot of different groups, if you're going to start laying down the law like this, you really are in danger of encouraging splits and breakaways," Friedman said.
Paul Perreira, a researcher at the South African Institute of Race Relations, said the ANC's handling of ructions in the provinces had shown how centralised power was in the party.
"If it uses pressure to quell dissent, all it does is close avenues for letting off steam, but eventually the dissent will come out one way or another," he said.
But Perreira said the ANC's strength meant it was unlikely that dissidents who left or were expelled would take large numbers of sympathisers with them.

Friedman said that in some areas like the Eastern Cape, a stronghold of ANC support, party members were drifting away because the first flush of enthusiasm that accompanied the dismantling of apartheid had dissipated.
"If these branches are withering on the vine, you're talking about a widening gap between government and the voters, which is a problem," he said.
Mandela told branch officials over the weekend that disappointing turn-out in last year's local government elections was a symptom of organisational problems.
"We need to be visibly involved, on a daily basis, in addressing the problems that affect each and every community," he said. "We cannot just become active and visible on the eve of an election."
